transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-20
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Zenith), Tom Baxter (Zenith), Priya Mehta (Zenith), Evan Li (Zenith)

Summary:
Quick SDK integration walkthrough for Redwood API + Console + Optimize. Focus on Python/TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns (API key vs SSO/SAML), environment setup (env vars, KMS), and POC next steps for dedicated trial and benchmarks.

Topics:
- SDK quickstarts (python + ts)
- Auth: API keys, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM
- Environment config: env vars, docker, private deployments (VPC)
- Redwood Console: routes, keys, rate limits, analytics
- Redwood Optimize: batching/quantization recommendations
- POC: datasets, metrics, timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Lena from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, quick intros?
[00:08] Aisha Khan: Hi all, Aisha here, director of eng at Zenith Retail, excited to see the SDKs, we've been evaluating a few options.
[00:13] Marco Ruiz: Marco Ruiz, solutions engineer, i'll be demoing integration snippets and setup, particularly python and typescript flows.
[00:20] Tom Baxter: Tom, backend lead, mostly concerned about auth and latency.
[00:24] Priya Mehta: Priya from security, i'll ask about keys, audit logs, KMS.
[00:28] Lena Park: Great. Agenda: quick overview, live walk through of the SDK quickstarts, auth patterns, console bits, and then POC details. Feel free to interject.

[00:45] Marco Ruiz: Alright starting with the Python quickstart, we have a small repo link - demo: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart (note: placeholder) - you can clone and run in a virtualenv. Main pattern is set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, pip install redwood-sdk, then import RedwoodClient. Example: client = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) then client.generate or client.chat.
[01:10] Tom Baxter: Is the SDK synchronous? We actually need streaming.
[01:13] Marco Ruiz: Yes we support streaming in both python and typescript. In python it's a .stream() call; in TS you can use the streaming client or Hornet-style event stream. There was a small transcription hiccup in the sample where it says hornet but it's actually event-source based.

[01:35] Evan Li: For typescript, do you recommend the SDK or raw HTTP? We have a node service.
[01:40] Marco Ruiz: SDK for convenience, it handles retries, structured outputs, and automatic KV prefix caching config. Raw HTTP is fine too if you want lightweight. The TS quickstart uses npm i @redwood/inference and env REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_BASE_URL if using Dedicated or Private.

[02:05] Priya Mehta: On auth, what's the recommended approach for us - api keys vs SSO? We have SAML SSO across org.
[02:12] Lena Park: For initial POC API keys are simplest, but for production we recommend SSO with RBAC provisioning and short-lived credentials. For Private deployments you can integrate with your IdP and KMS.
[02:23] Marco Ruiz: To add, we also support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for encryption at rest, and audit logs are available in the Console. We'll attach the KMS integration doc.

[02:45] Aisha Khan: Priya will want to see the SOC2 artifacts, and whether logs include token-level access.
[02:51] Marco Ruiz: Yes logs include token-level breakdown in Console, and trace ids for each request. We'll send the SOC2 summary and log retention options.

[03:10] Tom Baxter: Latency - for our use case we need sub-200ms 95p on short prompts, will we get that on hosted?
[03:17] Marco Ruiz: Depends on model size and request pattern. For short prompts many customers get <200ms 95p on our hosted smallest Llama-based curated model; for strict SLO you'd look at Dedicated with pinned capacity or local KV-cache tuning. We can run a quick benchmark in the POC.

[03:42] Lena Park: Quick demo of the console - i'll share my screen (note: demo referenced deck and console link). In Console you can create an API key, view usage, set route-level configs (model, timeout, fallback), and enable auto-batching suggestions from Optimize.
[04:00] Marco Ruiz: The Console also surfaces cost breakdown per route and token level, which helps evaluate tradeoffs between latency and cost.

[04:20] Evan Li: How does Optimize decide batching and quantization suggestions?
[04:25] Marco Ruiz: It analyses historical traffic patterns, sequence length distribution, and offers recommended batch sizes, quantization profile (int8 vs int4), and kernel choices for performance. It also simulates cost savings in the Console.

[04:45] Aisha Khan: For private deployments, network-wise, we require VPC peering and customer-managed subnets. Is that supported?
[04:51] Lena Park: Yes, our Private deployment supports VPC options and an on-prem package for air-gapped setups. We'll include the network checklist in the follow-up.

[05:10] Tom Baxter: Can you show the code sample for streaming in TS?
[05:13] Marco Ruiz: Sure - quick snippet:
const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
const stream = await client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-fast-chat-1', messages: [...] });
stream.on('data', chunk => { /* render chunk */ });
stream.on('end', () => console.log('done'));

[05:40] Evan Li: Any notable rate limits we should design for?
[05:43] Marco Ruiz: Default hosted limits are per-account but configurable; Dedicated gives predictable throughput, and Console exposes quotas. For POC we'll open higher rate windows.

[06:05] Aisha Khan: Ok can you explain how we would set environment variables securely in our CI?
[06:11] Marco Ruiz: Use your CI secret manager (GitHub Actions secrets, CircleCI env), avoid writing keys to logs. For extra security, use short-lived tokens from our SSO integration or inject via KMS-backed secrets manager.

[06:35] Priya Mehta: On audit: retention times and ability to export logs?
[06:39] Marco Ruiz: Yes, export via Console to S3 or SIEM, add retention policy per account. We'll include the log export how-to.

[07:00] Lena Park: Let's walk through a minimal python example - Marco?
[07:03] Marco Ruiz: Sure, python quickstart: pip install redwood-sdk
export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'])
resp = client.generate(model='redwood-small-1', prompt='Summarize latest order data')
print(resp.text)
Note: in the sample repo we have docker-compose and a sample .env.template.

[07:35] Tom Baxter: That looks straightforward. For the POC, we have a node-based microservice, would it be ok to route through our backend?
[07:41] Marco Ruiz: Absolutely. Common pattern is backend holds the API key and calls Redwood; if you need client-side features we recommend token minting via your backend for limited scope.

[08:00] Evan Li: Any SDK hooks for function calling / structured outputs?
[08:04] Marco Ruiz: Yes both SDKs support function/tool-calling and structured output parsing with schema enforcement. There's a small TS example in the quickstart showing a tool call to internal product search.

[08:30] Aisha Khan: We need to capture success metrics: P50/P95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, and quality checks against a set of prompts. Can Redwood integrate our evals?
[08:38] Marco Ruiz: Yes Redwood Optimize supports quality monitoring, you can upload prompt sets and expected outputs, and get regression alerts. We'll show the eval dashboard in the POC.

[09:00] Priya Mehta: For compliance we may need on-prem. How long does a Private deployment take?
[09:05] Lena Park: Typical timeline is 4-8 weeks depending on network approvals and environment readiness; on-prem can be longer. We'll provide an onboarding checklist.

[09:30] Tom Baxter: About model variants - can we fallback to cheaper models on overload?
[09:34] Marco Ruiz: Yes routing policies let you fallback by cost/latency - for example route to redwood-fast-chat for low latency, fallback to redwood-economy if capacity constrained.

[09:50] Lena Park: I'm going to share the quickstart repo link in chat and a doc that outlines the POC steps. (shared link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart)

[10:05] Marco Ruiz: Small note: some transcripts show 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache' - apologies for earlier voice-to-text errors. Our runtime uses KV cache to speed up repeated prefixes.

[10:25] Evan Li: For the benchmark, what test harness do you recommend?
[10:28] Marco Ruiz: We usually run a JMeter or locust script hitting the SDK or raw endpoint with realistic seq len distribution; we'll share our benchmark sheet template.

[10:45] Aisha Khan: Ok let's talk timeline - we want a 2-week POC with focused 3 endpoints and 1M tokens budget for test. Can you support that?
[10:52] Lena Park: Yes we can provision a trial Dedicated pool and open the quota. We'll need final dataset and success metrics by EOD Monday to provision.

[11:10] Priya Mehta: Does Redwood encrypt data in transit and at rest?
[11:14] Marco Ruiz: Yes TLS in transit and encryption at rest with optional customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM. Also support for bringing your own key for Private deployments.

[11:35] Tom Baxter: Are there SDK version compat issues we should be aware of?
[11:38] Marco Ruiz: We keep semver and publish changelogs; the quickstart pins a minor version and shows migration notes.

[11:55] Lena Park: Recap and next steps - we'll send SOC2 + KMS doc (Marco), SDK quickstart repo + code snippets (Lena), provision trial Dedicated and share admin creds (Lena + infra), Zenith to confirm dataset and metrics (Aisha).
[12:10] Aisha Khan: Sounds good, i'll confirm dataset and send calendar invite for follow-up.
[12:16] Evan Li: Thanks all.
[12:18] Marco Ruiz: Thanks everyone.

[12:25] Meeting end notes: References shared during call: quickstart repo (github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart), SOC2 summary (to be attached), benchmark template (sheet link placeholder), console screenshots. Some minor transcription errors expected in names and a few product terms.
